paras: The killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang was the pursuit and killing of a band of accused horse thieves by a farmers' vigilance committee in the Indian Territory in April 1888. Reports said that about eight members of the gang died, three of them killed after capture, and that one vigilante was shot dead. Papers nationwide called it a mass lynching; one California paper condemned killing men who had surrendered.

According to a Wichita dispatch, farmers in the Texas and Kansas counties bordering the Indian Territory had complained since the previous fall of bold raids by horse thieves. They formed a vigilance committee "for the purpose of exterminating the thieves" and rode out armed with Winchesters, six-shooters and lariats. A Purcell special added that the gang was the same one that had lost "old Bill Morgan" to vigilantes several days before.

After two weeks on the trail, the vigilantes came on the gang, led by Bill Higgins, alias "Scar Face," in a ravine in the western part of the Territory about ten days before April 20. One outlaw was shot dead as he mounted, and the rest fled in a running fight that lasted all day. The vigilantes drove the gang onto a butte near a small creek, where the outlaws' first volley killed Peter Ackerman of Medicine Lodge, Kansas.

At dusk a white rag was raised on the butte, and the vigilantes answered it with another volley and charged. Three outlaws escaped in the dark, while "Scar Face," Hank Windom and "Curly Bill" were "captured and killed." Curly Bill and Windom were shot, and Scar Face, nearly dead from loss of blood, was dragged to death by a lariat tied to a saddle. Four more members of the gang were found dead behind their stone barriers.

Shorter reports from Kansas City and Purcell told it differently, saying that eight thieves were surrounded and "shot or hanged," or "strung up without a chance to make confession," after a fight in which one of the posse died. They named Bill Higgle, alias "Scar-Face," and Curley Frank as the only dead men identified, and the Purcell special added an "Oliver Scarface."

No report of an inquest, arrests or any official action against the vigilantes appears in the coverage. The Purcell correspondent called the gang "the boldest set of cut-throats and thieves this section ever had to contend with."

From April 21 a brief from Kansas City and Purcell, headed "Eight Horse Thieves Lynched" in the Rock Island Argus and "A Wholesale Lynching Bee" in the Somerset Herald, was boiled down by digest columns to one line: "Eight horse thieves were lynched in the Indian Territory." That line appeared in the New-York Tribune, the Johnson City Comet and the Shepherdstown Register, and a version with "strung up without confession or prayers" ran in Michigan, Iowa and Chicago weeklies.

The longer Wichita narrative appeared in The Sun of New York, the San Antonio Daily Light, the Indianapolis Journal and the Memphis Appeal, and in weeklies into late May. Its text treated the dragging as "the true Western justice," while headline writers gave it the labels "LYNCH LAW" and "Death for Seven Men." Other weeklies headed the same text "Reads Like a Novel" and "Horse Thieves Done For," the latter as late as May 26 in Louisiana. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union said the farmers had done what any sheriff's posse would have done until the capture, but called the execution of three after surrender "a cruel, indefensible and a cowardly act."

Sheriff Dudley Reynolds of northern Texas, who reached Wichita on April 20, gave a different account, which the Charlotte Democrat printed as "a startling story of mob law." In his version the vigilantes fought the thieves twice, first in No Man's Land fifteen miles south of the Kansas line and then in northern Texas, with two vigilants and four thieves killed. Curly Bill died fighting from behind a dead horse, and only Scar Face was taken alive before a galloping horse dragged him by a rope around his neck. Totals for the dead also differed: eight in the briefs, seven or ten in headlines, while the Wichita text's own count comes to eight.

reader.title: Killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang, 1888
bases: Armed citizens described as a farmers' vigilance committee or posse pursued a band accused of horse stealing and, by the Wichita accounts, killed three men after capturing them, one dragged to death behind a horse (A4, A6, A21); the briefs call it the lynching of eight (A1, A2).

Every account has men killed by a citizens' band acting against accused horse thieves; the Wichita narrative says Scar Face, Windom and Curly Bill were 'captured and killed' after a white flag was raised, and the Sheriff Reynolds version has Scar Face captured alive and dragged to death (A4, A21), which A8 called execution after surrender. Some of the dead fell in a running gunfight, so not every death reported was a killing of a captive.

A Purcell special, a Kansas City report and two different Wichita dispatches agree that a citizens' band pursued and killed members of a horse-thief gang led by a man called Scar Face, with one vigilante killed (A2, A3, A4, A21), though they differ on numbers, place and how the captives died.

accounts.label: Kansas City report (deputy sheriff)
accounts.gist: A posse of citizens surprised eight horse thieves in southwestern Indian Territory; one of the posse was killed in a running fight, and the gang was surrounded and 'shot or hanged'.

accounts.label: Purcell special
accounts.gist: Confirmed the killing thirty miles southwest of Purcell; eight 'strung up without a chance to make confession', one of the posse killed; tied the gang to the earlier killing of Bill Morgan by vigilantes.

accounts.label: Wichita narrative
accounts.gist: A farmers' vigilance committee found the gang in a ravine, chased it to a butte, lost Peter Ackerman, and after a white flag charged; three outlaws escaped, Scar Face, Windom and Curly Bill were captured and killed, and four more were found dead.

accounts.label: Sheriff Dudley Reynolds
accounts.gist: Two fights, the first fifteen miles south of the Kansas line in No Man's Land and the second in northern Texas; two vigilants and four thieves killed, Curly Bill killed fighting, Scar Face captured alive and dragged by a galloping horse.

framing.detail: Digest papers ran a single line, 'Eight horse thieves were lynched in the Indian Territory,' without comment.

The Wichita narrative used labels such as 'marauders' and 'robbers' and called the dragging of Scar Face 'the true Western justice', while headline writers ran it as 'LYNCH LAW' or 'Death for Seven Men'.
The Purcell special called the gang 'the boldest set of cut-throats and thieves this section ever had to contend with'.
The Sacramento Record-Union defended the pursuit and battle as what a sheriff's posse would have done but called the execution of three after surrender 'cruel, indefensible and a cowardly act'.
The Charlotte Democrat headed Reynolds' account 'How the Vigilantes executed a notorious Horse Thief' and the text called it 'a startling story of mob law' and a 'horrible transaction'.

Eight gang members in the briefs and in the Wichita text's own count, plus one vigilante; headlines give seven or ten, and Reynolds four thieves and two vigilants.

Leader Bill Higgins alias 'Scar Face' (Bill Higgle in Kansas City/Purcell reports; 'Oliver Scarface' listed separately in the Omaha Bee), Hank Windom (Windsom, Winder), 'Curly Bill' (Wichita) or 'Curley Frank'/'Curly Frank' (Kansas City, Purcell); the rest unnamed.
Accused of being horse thieves who raided farms in Texas and Kansas counties bordering the Indian Territory.

A farmers' vigilance committee from Texas and Kansas border counties (Wichita narrative); 'a posse of citizens' (Kansas City, Rock Island); a 'Sheriff's posse' (Somerset Herald copy); settlers of southwest Kansas (Reynolds).
Three of the gang were reported to have escaped in the darkness.
